argument.name: Deriving the personal attributes of God and his relation to the world
argument.overview:
Feser gives no single numbered proof in this half of chapter 6. Instead he runs a series of short derivations, each starting from what the five proofs already secured — that God is **purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself, absolutely necessary, and unique**, and that everything else is composite, contingent, and dependent on him at every instant — and then applying three background principles from Part A: the **principle of proportionate causality** (PPC: whatever is in an effect is in its total cause formally, virtually, or eminently), **agere sequitur esse** (action follows being), and the **analogy of being**.

The reconstruction below lays those derivations out as one continuous line of reasoning. A recurring pattern is worth watching for: most attributes are reached by **two routes**, *backward* from the world as effect (via PPC or dependence) and *forward* from God's nature as pure act (via agere sequitur esse). Each stage also contains a **defensive step**, where Feser shows that the standard objection trades on a fallacy of accident or on treating God as a cause alongside other causes.

- Stages 1–4 derive **power, intellect and knowledge, goodness, will, freedom, and love**.
- Stage 5 explains why these results give real but incomplete knowledge (**incomprehensibility**).
- Stages 6–7 turn to **God's relation to the world**: conservation, concurrence, and miracles.
- Stage 8 is the short coda on **why God is called “he.”**

Step wording is a paraphrase and reconstruction, not Feser's own numbered formulation.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Omnipotence
stages.gist: Because everything depends on God for existence and therefore for action, and because subsistent existence can act in the fullest way, God has all power; ‘powers’ to do the contradictory are not powers at all.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Intellect and omniscience
stages.gist: By proportionate causality every feature of every possible thing is in God, and since not as instances nor in a Platonic realm, as concepts and propositions in an intellect; God meets every condition of knowledge and knows all by knowing himself as cause, in a unified, simple act.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Perfect goodness
stages.gist: Goodness is actuality in line with a thing's nature and badness a privation; so pure actuality is pure goodness, all good in creatures comes from God, and evil — being an absence — need not be in God.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Will, freedom, and love
stages.gist: An intellect that selects among possibles has will; nothing inside or outside God compels it, so it is free; no best world or obligation to create binds it; and willing the good of creatures just is love.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Incomprehensibility
stages.gist: Negative knowledge and literal analogy give real knowledge of God, but simplicity means he cannot be analyzed into parts, so full comprehension is impossible — as the arguments themselves predict.

stages.title: Stage 6 — Conservation and concurrence
stages.gist: God sustains all things at every instant yet is distinct from them; with action-follows-being this excludes both occasionalism and mere conservationism, leaving real secondary causes that act only with God's concurrence.

stages.title: Stage 7 — Miracles
stages.gist: Laws of nature express natures and cannot be violated, but God, who is not a cause among causes, can elevate nature beyond its powers or suspend an effect by withholding concurrence; such miracles can certify revelation.

stages.title: Stage 8 — Coda: speaking of God as ‘he’
stages.gist: God is sexless but personal, and his active, independent, distinct relation to the world resembles fatherhood more than motherhood.

steps.text: Everything other than God that exists or could exist is composite, a mixture of actuality and potentiality, has an essence distinct from its existence, and is contingent.
steps.why: Established by the five proofs and by the derivations of unity and simplicity in Part A: only the purely actual, simple, necessary being lacks these features, and there can be only one such being.

steps.text: Anything of that kind can exist even for an instant only if it is being caused to exist by the one purely actual, simple, necessary being who is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: This is the conclusion of the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs, all of which concern per se (here-and-now) causation, not a first push in the past.

steps.text: So everything other than God depends on God at every instant for its very existence.
steps.why: Follows directly from 1 and 2.

steps.text: Action follows being (agere sequitur esse): what a thing can do cannot exceed what it is, and existing is presupposed by acting.
steps.why: Defended in Part A as the formal-cause counterpart of proportionate causality, grounded in the principle of sufficient reason; acting that outran being would be unexplained.

steps.text: So everything other than God depends on God at every instant for its power to act as well as for its existence.
steps.why: From 3 and 4: if a thing has no independent capacity to exist, it cannot intelligibly have an independent capacity to act.

steps.text: Therefore nothing lies outside God's power and all power derives from him; that is, God is omnipotent (backward route).
steps.why: To be the source of all power, with nothing beyond its reach, is what ‘all-powerful’ means.

steps.text: God exists in the fullest possible way, and to have power is to be able to actualize potential.
steps.why: God is subsistent existence and pure act (from the proofs); to do or make just is to actualize some potential.

steps.text: So there is no actualizable potential God cannot actualize — omnipotence again (forward route).
steps.why: From 4 and 7: what exists in the fullest way acts in the fullest way, and nothing could possibly block such a being.

steps.text: Omnipotence does not include making round squares, a stone God cannot lift, or a sinning perfectly good being, because there are no such capacities to lack.
steps.why: Self-contradictory descriptions pick out nothing; since a stone's rising is always something that can occur, God can always cause it, so ‘a stone too heavy for God’ is as incoherent as a round square.

steps.text: Every thing, feature, and state of affairs that exists or could exist depends on God's causal activity at every moment.
steps.why: From 3 and 5.

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently (proportionate causality).
steps.why: Defended in Part A: an aspect of the effect that came from nothing in the cause would violate the principle of causality and the principle of sufficient reason.

steps.text: So every feature of every actual or possible thing — colors, shapes, chemical structures, powers of plants, animals, humans, angels — must be in God in some way.
steps.why: From 10 and 11.

steps.text: These features cannot be in God as instances, the way they are in creatures.
steps.why: God is immaterial; and more deeply, if God merely instantiated redness or roundness, his own instance would need explaining like any other, so he would not be the ultimate cause of red and round things.

steps.text: Universals are real, and apart from concrete instances they can exist only as concepts in an intellect or in a Platonic ‘third realm’; there is no such realm.
steps.why: Established in chapter 3 (the Augustinian proof), which rejected nominalism, conceptualism, and Platonism.

steps.text: So the forms of all things exist in God as concepts in an intellect: God has intellect.
steps.why: From 12, 13, and 14 by elimination.

steps.text: Likewise every state of affairs that obtains or could obtain exists in God as a proposition, including thoughts that given propositions are true or false.
steps.why: God causes not just the cat and the mat but the cat's being on the mat; a proposition is the intellectual correlate of a state of affairs as a concept is of a universal.

steps.text: To know p is (a) to think p true, (b) with p actually true, (c) as the result of a reliable process — understood analogically when applied to God.
steps.why: The standard philosophical account of knowledge, applied with the analogy of being from Part A.

steps.text: God meets all three conditions for each such proposition, so God has knowledge.
steps.why: (a) the thought is in his intellect (16); (b) it is true because he makes it so (10); (c) no process is more reliable than being the one who makes p true — as an author knows a character is in the story because he put him there.

steps.text: God also knows himself fully, so he knows every proposition about himself and everything else: he is omniscient.
steps.why: An author cannot know less of his own creative act than of the story; unlike a human author with an opaque body, God is simple, so nothing in him is hidden from his intellect. (The forward route was chapter 3's argument from an infinite intellect.)

steps.text: God knows the world not by observing it but by knowing himself as its cause, in a single timeless act.
steps.why: He is eternal (need not wait for events), incorporeal (no senses), and immutable (cannot learn). This blocks the inference to four-dimensionalism and shows his knowledge no more compels our acts than an author's writing compels a character — he is author, not hypnotist.

steps.text: Given simplicity, God's knowledge is not a collection of distinct thoughts but a unified knowledge of himself as pure actuality, which contains every limited way of being actual.
steps.why: As knowing white light perfectly would include knowing every color a prism could draw from it, or knowing the dough every cookie shape, knowing unlimited actuality includes knowing every finite kind.

steps.text: A thing is good, as a specimen of its kind, to the extent that it actualizes the potentials its nature directs it toward; moral goodness is the special case of free rational agents.
steps.why: Shown by the triangle (bus-seat scrawl vs. ruled drawing) and the tree (healthy vs. diseased roots): these judgments follow from natures, not preferences.

steps.text: So goodness is a kind of actuality, and badness is a privation — the absence of an actuality a thing's nature calls for.
steps.why: A wavy side is a privation in a triangle, a missing fourth side is not; weak roots are a privation in a tree, missing wings are not. Goodness is primary; badness, like blindness, is a lack.

steps.text: The privation account withstands its main objections.
steps.why: It explains rather than denies evil's reality; pain is bad only by association (it can be useful or satisfying; cf. pain asymbolia); a murderer's positive desires may be good in themselves, the badness lying in what his intention lacks; sadism is desire misdirected, a psychological deformity.

steps.text: God is pure actuality with no unrealized potential.
steps.why: From the Aristotelian proof and Part A.

steps.text: So God is purely good, with no badness of any kind (forward route).
steps.why: From 23 and 25.

steps.text: And since all good in the world must be in its cause, God is the source of all possible good and in that sense all-good (backward route).
steps.why: From 11 applied to goodness.

steps.text: Proportionate causality does not put evil in God, and permitting evil is compatible with his goodness.
steps.why: Evil is an absence, not a positive feature, so making a world with evil is making goods while refraining from others (the unfinished triangle); some goods, such as courage, are impossible without real danger, just as round squares are impossible.

steps.text: Every nature inclines toward its fulfillment: unconsciously in plants, with sensory appetite in animals, with rational appetite (will) in intellectual beings.
steps.why: The tree, the dog, and the human being illustrate the three grades of appetite.

steps.text: Since God has intellect, there is in him something analogous to will: the limit case of rational appetite, by which he wills some possibles to exist and not others.
steps.why: He ‘rests’ in his fully realized nature rather than striving (like zero km/s as the limit case of speed); and he grasps all possibles yet causes only some, which is analogous to willing.

steps.text: Nothing external can compel God's will.
steps.why: Everything other than God depends on him for existence and action at every instant (3, 5).

steps.text: Nothing internal compels it either.
steps.why: No concept in the divine intellect (lion, unicorn) contains any necessity that its instances exist or not; before creation either world was equally possible.

steps.text: So God's will is free.
steps.why: From 31 and 32: freedom from all external and internal compulsion.

steps.text: Neither simplicity nor perfect goodness removes this freedom.
steps.why: Freedom as such does not require actualizing potentials (to assume so is a fallacy of accident); no one is wronged if God does not create; there is no best possible world (always x + 1 forests); and God's perfection follows from what he is, not what he makes (the diamond that need not cut any glass).

steps.text: What is essential to love is willing the good of the beloved, not being emotionally affected.
steps.why: Hence shallow love is mere fluctuating feeling, while serious love, tough love, and love of enemies persist in willing the good against feeling; will is active, emotion passive.

steps.text: To create is to actualize, and so to will that a thing exist together with the goods that flow from its nature.
steps.why: Goodness is actuality (23); willing trees exist is willing their roots, nourishment, and photosynthesis.

steps.text: So God loves what he creates, and does so without any change in him.
steps.why: From 30, 35, and 36; the objection that love requires changeability is a fallacy of accident.

steps.text: Negative (apophatic) knowledge of God is real knowledge, and positive attributes are predicated of him literally by analogy of attribution and of proper proportionality.
steps.why: God is the primary analogate of power (the sun's power is derived); a tree, a human, an angel, and God are each to their own goodness in proportionally similar ways, God's being the limit case.

steps.text: So in a loose sense we genuinely comprehend God; the position is neither fideist nor purely negative.
steps.why: From 38 and the fact that we understand the book's arguments.

steps.text: Comprehension in the strict sense works by analyzing a thing into its parts, or into genus and specific difference.
steps.why: This is how we come to understand material systems and even immaterial natures.

steps.text: Since God is absolutely simple, he cannot be comprehended in the strict sense; the mystery is predicted by the arguments themselves, not a retreat into obscurantism.
steps.why: From 40 and simplicity; compare physics, which must speak strangely (wave-particles, curved space) far from everyday experience.

steps.text: God conserves every created thing in being at every instant; creation is ongoing, and nothing contingent has ‘existential inertia.’
steps.why: From 2 and 3; anything composite of act and potency or of essence and existence needs a sustaining cause, and the inertia thesis never explains how a contingent thing could lack that need.

steps.text: Yet created things are really distinct from God, so pantheism and panentheism are false.
steps.why: They are composite, potential, essence-distinct-from-existence, and contingent; he is simple, pure act, subsistent existence, necessary, and immutable (so not changed by the world).

steps.text: Occasionalism (only God causes) is false.
steps.why: By action-follows-being, what does nothing is nothing, so only God would exist; but you exist and are not God (you change, doubt, and lack power). And it destroys the premises about real, changing, composite things that led us to God — pulling away the ladder.

steps.text: Mere conservationism (creatures act independently once sustained) is false.
steps.why: By action-follows-being, whatever could act independently could exist independently — essentially deism; but nothing composite can exist without conservation, and this view too undermines the proofs' starting point.

steps.text: Concurrentism is true: created things are genuine but secondary causes, making a real contribution to their effects while able to act only as God concurs with them.
steps.why: The only position left once both extremes fail; illustrated by the blue chalk (you make the square, the chalk its blueness) and the moon (its look is its own, its light is the sun's).

steps.text: Among these secondary causes are free human agents.
steps.why: Human beings are creatures conserved and concurred with like any other.

steps.text: God's concurrence does not destroy human freedom.
steps.why: Like a father guiding his son's hand to write an A: the boy's cooperation or resistance is a real contribution, but no letter appears without the father's guidance.

steps.text: Laws of nature describe the dispositions things have by virtue of their natures; dispositions can be blocked or lack their triggers.
steps.why: The Aristotelian account of laws (Ramelow, Oderberg): water's disposition to freeze at 32°F, which unusual conditions can prevent.

steps.text: So, given that the things exist, laws are metaphysically necessary and cannot be violated; the Humean definition of a miracle as a violation is mistaken.
steps.why: Different laws would mean different natures, hence different things (whatever turned to mousse at 32°F would not be water); if triggers are present and nothing blocks, the manifestation follows.

steps.text: A miracle is an effect that elevates a thing beyond what any created nature can account for: supernatural, as opposed to subnatural (defects) or preternatural (what angels might do).
steps.why: Ramelow's Thomistic definition.

steps.text: Only God can work miracles, and in doing so he does not ‘intervene,’ since he is not a cause alongside the others but the source of all causal power, already causing the ordinary course.
steps.why: From 5, 46, and 51; McCabe: God cannot interfere, not for lack of power, but because he is alongside nothing.

steps.text: A miracle may add to nature (resurrection, loaves) or subtract from it (the fiery furnace) — the latter by God refraining from conserving or concurring with some factors, which is a suspension rather than a breach of the law.
steps.why: From 42, 46, and 50: withholding concurrence means the normal effect simply does not arise; nothing is forced to act against its nature.

steps.text: Therefore miracles are possible.
steps.why: From 52 and 53.

steps.text: If God willed to reveal truths reason cannot reach, a miracle worked by his messenger would be the fitting divine ‘seal’ on the message, since only God can work one.
steps.why: From 52: no creature can counterfeit a strictly supernatural effect.

steps.text: Miracles are the bridge from natural to revealed theology: they ground faith in reason, and natural theology tests any religion's claims about God.
steps.why: Faith is believing because God has revealed; that he has revealed needs miraculous evidence. Religions that make God many, identical with the world, impersonal, material, or finite — or that claim revelation without miracle — are thereby discredited.

steps.text: God is not an animal and so not literally male or female, but he has intellect and will, which define personhood.
steps.why: Immateriality (Part A) and stages 2 and 4.

steps.text: God's relation to the world — active, unchanged, independent, distinct — resembles a father's role in procreation more than a mother's.
steps.why: The father acts, is unchanged, is not physically dependent, and is not physically continuous with the child; the mother is changed and continuous with the child.

steps.text: So personal, paternal (masculine) language is the least misleading way to speak of God; ‘it’ denies his personhood and maternal imagery suggests pantheism or panentheism.
steps.why: From 57 and 58.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of having all power: being the source of every power anything has, with no actualizable potential beyond one's ability to actualize.
keyTerms.example: God can cause any possible state of affairs, such as a stone's rising, but ‘making a round square’ names no possible state of affairs and so no power.

keyTerms.definition: Latin, ‘action follows being’: what a thing does reflects and cannot exceed what it is.
keyTerms.example: Because creatures cannot exist on their own, they cannot act on their own; because God is existence itself, he can act in every way.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently.
keyTerms.example: Every feature of every possible creature must be in God somehow — which, Feser argues, means as ideas in an intellect.

keyTerms.definition: Three ways an effect's feature can be in a cause: as the same form (formally), as a power to produce it (virtually), or in a higher way that contains the power to produce it (eminently).
keyTerms.example: A $20 bill in my wallet (formally), $20 in my bank account (virtually), a Federal Reserve printing press (eminently).

keyTerms.definition: The puzzle: can God make a stone too heavy for him to lift? Either way, something seems beyond him.
keyTerms.example: Dissolved because ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is self-contradictory, like a round square.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of all propositions about oneself and everything else that is or could be.
keyTerms.example: God knows the cat is on the mat because he knows himself as causing the cat to be on the mat.

keyTerms.definition: S knows p when S thinks p is true, p is true, and S's thinking so comes from a reliable process.
keyTerms.example: God meets each condition analogically; making p true is the most reliable way of ‘finding out’ that p.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing something by knowing oneself as its cause, rather than by perceiving it.
keyTerms.example: An author knows his characters by knowing his own intentions, not by watching them.

keyTerms.definition: The view that past, present, and future all exist and time is a spacelike fourth dimension.
keyTerms.example: Feser denies that timeless divine knowledge implies it — just as a motionless hunter's instant knowledge doesn't make the bullet motionless.

keyTerms.definition: Feser's contrast between a cause outside the story (compatible with characters' freedom) and a cause inside the story that interferes with others (incompatible with their freedom).
keyTerms.example: The crime novel's murderer acts freely though the author wrote him; not so if another character hypnotized him.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a thing actualizes the potentials its nature or essence directs it toward.
keyTerms.example: A carefully ruled triangle is a good triangle; a tree with deep roots is a good tree.

keyTerms.term: Privation (and the privation theory of evil)
keyTerms.definition: The absence of something a thing ought to have given its nature, as opposed to a mere absence; the classical theory holds that all badness, evil included, is a privation of due good rather than a positive reality.
keyTerms.example: Blindness in a dog is a privation, while a tree's lacking wings is not; the badness of a murder lies in the missing intention to seek gain only by just means.

keyTerms.definition: A condition caused by certain brain damage in which pain is felt without its usual unpleasantness.
keyTerms.example: Cited as evidence that what is bad is not pain itself but what accompanies it.

keyTerms.definition: Conscious inclination toward ends apprehended by the senses, found in animals.
keyTerms.example: A dog seeking food and water.

keyTerms.definition: Inclination toward what the intellect grasps as worth pursuing (and away from what it grasps as not).
keyTerms.example: A human choosing a career because he judges it worthwhile; analogously, God willing some possibles to exist.

keyTerms.definition: (From Barry Miller) Something toward which a series points but which differs absolutely, not merely in degree, from the members of the series.
keyTerms.example: Zero km/s is not the slowest speed but no speed; the divine will and divine goodness are limit cases of creaturely appetite and goodness.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that what usually accompanies something in our experience is essential to it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Our love involves emotional change, so love as such requires change.’

keyTerms.definition: A hypothetical world than which no better could exist; Leibniz held God must create it.
keyTerms.example: Feser denies there is one: for any world with x forests there is a possible world with x + 1.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of God by denying creaturely limitations of him: not composite, not changing, not material, not temporal.
keyTerms.example: Feser counts it real knowledge, though not the whole story.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically to a primary analogate and to secondary analogates by their relation to it.
keyTerms.example: God is the primary analogate of ‘power’; the sun has power only as derived from him.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically and literally to several things because each stands in a proportionally similar relation.
keyTerms.example: A tree is to its goodness as a human to his, an angel to his, and God to his.

keyTerms.definition: The impossibility of fully grasping God's nature, since simplicity leaves no parts or genus-difference structure to analyze.
keyTerms.example: We know truly that God is good, but cannot grasp what his goodness is in itself.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God keeps every creature in existence at every instant; without him it would be instantly annihilated.
keyTerms.example: Creation is not a past event but happening now.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that some things, once existing, persist on their own until destroyed, needing no conserving cause.
keyTerms.example: Feser: never explained, and impossible for anything composite of act and potency or essence and existence.

keyTerms.definition: The view that only God causes anything; creatures are merely occasions on which he acts.
keyTerms.example: God, not the sun, melts the ice; God, not the cue ball, moves the eight ball.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God keeps things in being but they exercise causal power independently of him.
keyTerms.example: God sustains the sun, but the sun melts the ice on its own — a view Feser says collapses into deism.

keyTerms.definition: The view that creatures are real but secondary causes that can act only as God, the primary cause, concurs with their action.
keyTerms.example: You and the blue chalk jointly cause a blue square — you the square, the chalk the blueness.

keyTerms.definition: A genuine cause that makes a real contribution to its effect but whose causal power is derived from and dependent on the first cause.
keyTerms.example: The moon lights the night sky with its own look, but only by the sun's light.

keyTerms.definition: Supernatural: beyond the power of any created nature (only God); preternatural: extraordinary but within the power of created natures such as angels; subnatural: falling short of a nature, a defect.
keyTerms.example: A resurrection is supernatural; an angel's feat would be preternatural; a two-headed calf is subnatural.

keyTerms.definition: Oderberg's distinction: a breach leaves the law in force but unenforced; a suspension temporarily removes the law.
keyTerms.example: The fiery furnace: God withholds his concurrence from the fire, so the burning simply does not arise.
